items.stem: Which of the following best describes "climate tipping point"?
options: The likely changes in hazards, exposure and vulnerability over coming decades due to population, urbanisation, climate and global interactions
A critical threshold beyond which a part of the climate system changes abruptly and often irreversibly, e.g. collapse of an ice sheet
Discarded electronic equipment, often exported to lower-income countries for processing
Smoke from forest and peat fires that spreads across borders, as in South-East Asia
items.answer: A critical threshold beyond which a part of the climate system changes abruptly and often irreversibly, e.g. collapse of an ice sheet
items.markingKey: B. "climate tipping point" is a critical threshold beyond which a part of the climate system changes abruptly and often irreversibly, e.g. collapse of an ice sheet.

items.stem: Distinguish between gradual climate change and abrupt change at tipping points.
items.answer: Gradual change increases roughly in proportion to warming; abrupt change occurs suddenly once a threshold is crossed and may be irreversible.
items.markingKey: Gradual change increases roughly in proportion to warming; abrupt change occurs suddenly once a threshold is crossed and may be irreversible. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Lars writes: "Exporting waste solves the problem for rich countries." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: It shifts environmental and health risks to poorer countries and plastics return through oceans and food chains.

items.stem: Tide-gauge records at Venice show mean sea level of 7009 mm (relative to a local datum) in 1990 and 7162 mm in 2010. Calculate the mean rate of relative sea-level rise.
items.answer: 7.7 mm per year

items.stem: With reference to the 2015 South-East Asian haze, explain how it illustrates transboundary air pollution.
items.answer: Fires in Indonesia sent smoke across Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand, closing schools and harming health. Land clearance in one country created health risks across a region.

items.stem: Tide-gauge records at Lagos show mean sea level of 7067 mm (relative to a local datum) in 1990 and 7361 mm in 2015. Calculate the mean rate of relative sea-level rise. Project the additional rise over the next 50 years at this rate, and explain why the rate here may differ from the global mean (about 3.7 mm/yr recently).
items.answer: 11.8 mm/yr; ≈ 59 cm in 50 years; local subsidence (groundwater pumping, delta compaction), tectonics or ocean circulation alter relative rise.
items.markingKey: A1 11.8 mm/yr; A1 588 mm; R1 R1 relative vs eustatic explanation.

items.stem: Outline one argument for and one argument against the view that the Paris Agreement will prevent dangerous climate change.
items.answer: It is unlikely to prevent dangerous change on current pledges without much stronger action.
items.markingKey: For: universal participation and ratchet mechanism. Against: current pledges imply about 2.5-2.9 °C. [4]: 1 mark for a valid argument for, 1 for its development; 1 mark for a valid argument against, 1 for its development; generic points without geographical context are capped at 2.

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that future geophysical hazard risk will be determined more by human factors than by physical processes?
items.answer: Physical processes are constant, so changing human exposure and vulnerability will largely determine future risk.
items.markingKey: Indicative content - for: urbanisation and exposure growing fast; governance and building quality. Against / limitations: major events (Cascadia, Tokyo, Istanbul) are inevitable; climate change increases secondary hazards. A supported conclusion might be: Physical processes are constant, so changing human exposure and vulnerability will largely determine future risk. items.stem: Examine the view that climate tipping points are the greatest environmental risk facing the world.
items.answer: Tipping points may be the most catastrophic risk long term, but current pollution causes greater immediate harm.
items.markingKey: Indicative content - for: irreversible, abrupt and global effects; positive feedbacks. Against / limitations: air pollution kills about 7 million people a year now; biodiversity loss and water scarcity also severe. items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Discarded electronic equipment, often exported to lower-income countries for processing"?
options: e-waste
cascading risk
transboundary pollution
Great Pacific Garbage Patch
items.answer: e-waste
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of e-waste.

items.stem: Under the Paris Agreement, emissions targets are:
options: set by the UN for each country and legally enforced with fines
set by each country as nationally determined contributions
only required of developing countries
the same for every country
items.answer: set by each country as nationally determined contributions
items.markingKey: B. They are reviewed in five-year cycles (the ratchet mechanism).

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The likely changes in hazards, exposure and vulnerability over coming decades due to population, urbanisation, climate and global interactions"?
options: Global Plastics Treaty
future risk
transboundary pollution
systems thinking
items.answer: future risk
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of future risk.

items.stem: A student claims: "Pollution stops at national borders." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Air, rivers and oceans carry pollution across borders and around the world.
items.markingKey: Air, rivers and oceans carry pollution across borders and around the world. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between the Montreal Protocol and the Paris Agreement.
items.answer: The Montreal Protocol has binding phase-out schedules for a few specific chemicals and near-universal compliance; the Paris Agreement relies on voluntary national pledges covering all greenhouse gases from the whole economy.
items.markingKey: The Montreal Protocol has binding phase-out schedules for a few specific chemicals and near-universal compliance; the Paris Agreement relies on voluntary national pledges covering all greenhouse gases from the whole economy. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Kenji writes: "Geophysical hazards only have local impacts." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Through global networks, local events can disrupt worldwide supply chains, air travel and financial markets.
items.markingKey: Through global networks, local events can disrupt worldwide supply chains, air travel and financial markets. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain the difference between local pollution and transboundary pollution.
items.answer: Local pollution affects the area where it is produced; transboundary pollution crosses national borders, so management requires international cooperation.
items.markingKey: Local pollution affects the area where it is produced; transboundary pollution crosses national borders, so management requires international cooperation. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "The Paris Agreement legally requires countries to meet their targets." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Countries must submit and report on NDCs, but meeting them is not legally enforced.
items.markingKey: Countries must submit and report on NDCs, but meeting them is not legally enforced. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why global interactions can also increase resilience to hazards.
items.answer: They provide access to aid, expertise, insurance and reinsurance markets, technology such as early warning and satellites, and alternative suppliers, allowing faster recovery.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They provide access to aid, expertise, insurance and reinsurance markets, technology such as early warning and satellites, and alternative suppliers, allowing faster recovery. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Between 2005 and 2020 the area of Arctic summer (September) sea ice measured by a satellite record changed from 5.6 to 4.5 million km². Calculate the percentage change over the period.
items.markingKey: M1 (new − old) ÷ old × 100 = (4.5 − 5.6) ÷ 5.6 × 100; A1 -19.6% (sign or "increase/decrease" required).

items.answer: e.g. Eyjafjallajökull 2010: ash closed European airspace for six days; about 100,000 flights cancelled; Kenyan flower and vegetable exports to Europe were stranded, costing growers about US$1.3 million a day; global airlines lost about US$1.7 billion.

items.stem: A cement plant covered by the EU ETS (allowance price) emits 54,000 t CO₂ per year. The carbon price is about € 85 per tonne. Calculate the annual carbon cost, and the saving if the plant cuts emissions by 20%.

The following information is provided.

Data: during the 2010 Eyjafjallajökull ash closure, Kenya's horticulture sector lost about US$1.3 million per day for 6 days, and airlines lost about US$200 million per day for 6 days.

Explain why an eruption in Iceland affected farmers in Kenya.
items.answer: Kenyan flowers and vegetables are air-freighted to Europe in just-in-time supply chains; closed airspace stranded perishable goods.

items.stem: Tide-gauge records at Miami show mean sea level of 7002 mm (relative to a local datum) in 1970 and 7164 mm in 1995. Calculate the mean rate of relative sea-level rise. Project the additional rise over the next 75 years at this rate, and explain why the rate here may differ from the global mean (about 3.7 mm/yr recently).
items.answer: 6.5 mm/yr; ≈ 49 cm in 75 years; local subsidence (groundwater pumping, delta compaction), tectonics or ocean circulation alter relative rise.
items.markingKey: A1 6.5 mm/yr; A1 486 mm; R1 R1 relative vs eustatic explanation.
